name: Agastheeswarar Temple, Kiliyanur (Thirukkiliyannavur)
deity: Shiva as Agastheeswarar, with the Goddess Akhilandeswari
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, sung by Sambandar (7th century); rebuilt in stone under Parantaka Chola I
summary: On the road from Tindivanam to Puducherry, the village of Kiliyanur keeps the Lord whom the sage Agastya worshipped — a Tevaram shrine of Sambandar, rebuilt in granite by the early Cholas.

sections.history: Kiliyanur is a village of Villupuram district on the road between Tindivanam and Puducherry, and its temple is the Thirukkiliyannavur of the Tevaram. Dedicated to Shiva as Agastheeswarar, it is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu; Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord in a pathigam preserved in the third Tirumurai. The shrine is held to be very old, and inscriptions within the temple are said to record that it was first built of brick and then raised again in granite in the reign of the Chola king Parantaka I in the tenth century — the familiar story of a Tevaram shrine renewed in stone under the early Cholas.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest Dravidian shrine of the coastal plain, with the lingam of Agastheeswarar in the sanctum and the Goddess Akhilandeswari in a shrine of her own. The vanni tree is honoured as the sthala vriksham. The granite fabric of the sanctum, with its inscriptions, carries the record of the Chola rebuilding that replaced the earlier brick temple.
sections.legends: The Lord takes his name from Agastya, the great sage of the south, who is said to have worshipped Shiva here. The sthala purana adds that the sage Sukha Brahma came here suffering a severe ailment of the stomach and was healed by his worship, and that Adisesha, the serpent on whom Vishnu rests, also offered worship at this shrine. A tradition of the temple holds that on the night of Maha Shivaratri, Nandi himself comes to worship the Goddess Akhilandeswari.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great night of the year here, with the monthly pradosham, the Navaratri festival of the Goddess and the customary Shaiva observances; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Kiliyanur is an easy stop on the busy Tindivanam–Puducherry road, yet the temple itself is quiet. Devotees seeking relief from illness pray here in memory of the healed sage, and those following the Tevaram shrines of Nadu Nadu combine it with Thiruvakkarai and the temples around Villupuram.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure; village temples may close early in the evening. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Kiliyanur lies about 18 km from Tindivanam on the road to Puducherry, which is about 20 km further south-east; buses between the two towns stop at the village. Tindivanam has the nearest railway station, with Villupuram the nearest major junction; Puducherry has the closest airport, and Chennai the nearest major international airport.
